title: The Supreme Court Said Vinesh Phogat Can Wrestle. The Federation Said She Could Not.
excerpt: India's three-time Olympian was barred from Asian Games selection trials after a maternity break. The Delhi High Court and then the Supreme Court overruled the Wrestling Federation, saying motherhood is not a disability.
body:
Vinesh Phogat, India's most decorated wrestler still in active competition, was told she could not try out for the 2026 Asian Games. The Wrestling Federation of India said she had not participated in the mandatory qualifying tournaments. Phogat said she had been on maternity leave.

The case went to the Delhi High Court, then to the Supreme Court, and in both places the answer was the same: let her compete.

On May 29, a bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe refused to stay a Delhi High Court order that had cleared Phogat to participate in the Asian Games selection trials scheduled for May 30-31 at New Delhi's Indira Gandhi Stadium.

**"If it were anybody else, it would have been on a different footing. She has made the country proud,"** the bench said during the hearing. "We are not stopping you. Go and participate."

## The Policy That Excluded Her

Earlier this year, the WFI issued a circular mandating that only medal winners from the 2025 National Championship, the 2026 Federation Cup, and the U20 National Championship would be eligible for Asian Games selection trials. No exceptions.

Phogat had announced a sabbatical in December 2024. She gave birth in July 2025 and informed the WFI she would be eligible to compete from January 2026. By the time she was ready to return, the qualifying windows had closed.

Her legal team, led by Senior Advocate Shyam Divan, argued that the policy was tailored to exclude her. "In the past, they have always given exceptions to iconic players," Divan told the court. "Women face this problem. There is a natural disadvantage. This was tailor-made to exclude her."

The WFI countered that Phogat had never applied for an exemption and that the rules applied uniformly. But the Supreme Court was unpersuaded. "High Court having passed the order, to tell her to go back home will not be proper," Justice Narasimha said. "Everything is not legal-based."

## Motherhood Is Not a Barrier

The Delhi High Court's May 22 ruling, which the Supreme Court chose not to disturb, went further than simply allowing Phogat to compete. Justice Tejas Karia wrote that the WFI's selection policy appeared exclusionary because it did not provide sufficient discretion to consider an "iconic player" returning after a maternity break.

"It cannot be denied that the journey of a female athlete through pregnancy and the post-partum period is one that is marked by extraordinary physical challenges, the magnitude of which is often insufficiently acknowledged within institutional sporting frameworks," the High Court observed. "We cannot remain oblivious to the physiological realities and disadvantages related to childbirth that female athletes undergo during maternity."

The court directed the WFI to video-record the selection trials and appointed independent observers from the Sports Authority of India and the Indian Olympic Association to ensure transparency.

## Doping Questions Linger

The Supreme Court did not ignore complications in Phogat's case. During the hearing, questions were raised about missed doping tests. Phogat's counsel explained that the 12-month window for whereabouts failures had not expired and that she had provided a test in January 2026. The bench noted the issue but did not let it override the broader question of participation.

The WFI's plea remains pending and will be heard in detail next week. But the immediate question — whether Phogat could step on the mat for trials — was settled.

## The Larger Context

Vinesh Phogat's career has been defined by fights on and off the mat. She was among the wrestlers who led protests against the then-president of the Wrestling Federation of India in 2023, accusing him of sexual harassment — a scandal that led to his arrest and the federation's suspension by the Indian Olympic Association.

At the 2024 Paris Olympics, Phogat was disqualified from the gold medal bout in the 50 kg category after being found overweight by 100 grams on the morning of the final. She challenged the decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which denied her appeal.

For the Indian diaspora, Phogat's saga resonates as a story about institutional resistance to women who refuse to comply quietly. The Supreme Court's refusal to stop her from competing — even as it acknowledged the WFI's procedural concerns — was a statement that the rules must make room for life.
